analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from evicting tenants without a court order during federally declared emergencies.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2021 with three Democratic cosponsors, the bill went to a House Judiciary subcommittee in April 2021 and never got a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal violation for a landlord, during a nationally declared emergency, to remove a tenant without a court order, harass or intimidate them into leaving, or cut utilities and skip repairs to force them out. Tenants could sue for triple damages and attorney's fees, and the Justice Department could sue on their behalf, with penalties split between the tenant, a DOJ enforcement fund, and the Legal Services Corporation. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee, and died there without ever getting a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters living in areas covered by a federally declared emergency. They would have gained a federal right to a judge's order before eviction, plus the ability to recover triple damages and attorney's fees if a landlord locked them out, cut their utilities, harassed them, or stopped repairs to push them out. Tenants who could not afford a lawyer would also have benefited from the share of penalties directed to the Legal Services Corporation for fair-housing legal work. The bill was introduced in March 2021, while the COVID-19 emergency was in effect.

how_it_helps.text: During a nationally declared emergency, a landlord could not repossess a dwelling without a court order, threaten or harass a tenant to make them leave, or impair habitability — for example by suspending utilities, changing locks, or refusing to repair plumbing, electrical, or structural systems — to force a tenant out.

Tenants harmed by a violation could sue for an injunction, return of the property, and damages equal to three times their injury or three times the rent charged after the violation, plus attorney's fees; the Attorney General could also sue on a tenant's behalf.

Damages recovered by the Attorney General would be split three ways: to the victim, to a DOJ fund for future enforcement actions, and to the Legal Services Corporation to support fair-housing legal services — creating a funding stream for tenant legal help.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords. Any owner of a covered dwelling who knowingly carried out a self-help eviction, harassed a tenant into leaving, or degraded the unit to push them out during a declared emergency would face civil suits, triple damages, and attorney-fee awards, and could be sued by the Justice Department as well.
analysis.who_pays_short: Landlords who evict without court orders

drawbacks.text: The protections are narrow: they only apply in areas the President has designated as a national emergency, and only for the duration of that designation — tenants get no federal protection once the emergency declaration ends.

The penalty is steep and open-ended: a violating landlord owes the greater of triple the injury or triple all rent charged after the violation, plus attorney's fees — a level of exposure that landlord groups and small landlords would say raises the cost and risk of renting, especially in disaster-prone areas where the Stafford Act trigger applies.

Enforcement depends on individual tenants suing or the Attorney General choosing to act, and a third of DOJ-recovered damages would flow into a DOJ fund usable without further appropriation — a self-funding enforcement structure that gives the department its own financial stake in bringing cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For tenants, the benefit would have been real and concrete: many states still permit some form of self-help eviction, and even where it is illegal, penalties are often weak, so a federal court-order requirement with triple damages and fee-shifting would have given renters meaningful leverage during emergencies like the COVID-19 pandemic. The costs fall on landlords, and the treble-damages formula keyed to all rent charged could produce large judgments, but the strongest design criticism is not the penalty — it is the coverage: the protections switch off the moment a national emergency designation ends, and enforcement hinges on tenants or the DOJ acting. On balance, a modest, targeted bill whose main weakness was that it never got a chance to be amended or debated.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee referred it to its Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties subcommittee in April 2021, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on March 1, 2021, with Rep. Ilhan Omar and Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton as original cosponsors; it had three Democratic cosponsors in total and no Republican support.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on April 28, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties.

No further action was ever taken: the subcommittee never held a hearing or markup, the full committee never voted, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners are better off because the bill died: no federal penalty now exists for removing tenants without a court order, cutting utilities, or harassing them out during a declared national emergency, and landlords face no treble-damages exposure under this law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords; the bill died in committee

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Emergency Eviction Enforcement Act of 2021 on March 1, 2021.

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar and Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill drew three Democratic cosponsors in total.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jerrold Nadler)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties on April 28, 2021; the subcommittee and full committee never held a hearing or markup, and no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no split can be measured; the bill's sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican ever signed on.

industries.industry: Landlords and residential rental property owners
industries.note: The bill would have stripped landlords' ability to reclaim a unit through lockouts, utility shutoffs, harassment, or neglect during a declared emergency, exposing violators to triple damages and attorney-fee awards. Their interest in evicting without court process runs directly against tenants' ability to stay housed.

industries.industry: Legal Services Corporation and legal aid providers
industries.note: One-third of damages recovered by the Attorney General would have gone to the Legal Services Corporation for fair-housing work, adding a dedicated funding stream for tenant legal representation.
